title: Comprehension · curated QnA gold + narrative reference prose
disclosure: Comprehension (default discursive track). Amateur exercise — not medical validity. Same Clinical Composite dimensions as optional Structured A1–A5; never pool Histories. Acute ED-biased pack Case 1–10 (AKI/hyperK, anaphylaxis, STEMI, DKA, stroke, OD, psychosis/delirium, septic shock, PE, UGIB). Provenance: vignettes assembled with Cursor and/or adapted from public internet teaching material — not validated EHR charts. Scored gold = curated gold_raw Q1–A5; reference_prose is narrative twin.

1.title: AKI with critical hyperkalemia
1.stem:
Patient: 58-year-old male.
History: Medical history positive for long-standing hypertension treated chronically with an ACE-inhibitor. Presents to the Emergency Department with altered mental status (confusion) that developed over the last 36 hours, severe fatigue, and marked oliguria. He also reports diffuse abdominal pain and paresthesias in his lower extremities.
Physical Examination: Pale, cold, and clammy skin. Blood pressure 85/50 mmHg (marked hypotension), heart rate 52 bpm with a noticeably irregular rhythm. Abdomen is distended and minimally tender to palpation. Deep tendon reflexes are reduced in the lower extremities.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Serum Creatinine: 4.2 mg/dL (baseline value from one month ago: 0.9 mg/dL). BUN (Blood Urea Nitrogen): 98 mg/dL. Serum Potassium (K⁺): 7.8 mEq/L (critical hyperkalemia). Serum Sodium: 132 mEq/L. Venous Blood Gas (VBG): pH 7.21, HCO₃⁻ 14 mmol/L (metabolic acidosis with a normal/elevated anion gap). Electrocardiogram (ECG): Tall, peaked ("tented") T waves, widening of the QRS complex, loss of P waves, and severe bradycardia with junctional escape rhythms.
1.reference_prose: This is severe acute kidney injury (KDIGO stage 3) with critical hyperkalemia and ECG signs of potassium cardiotoxicity in a hypotensive, oliguric patient on a chronic ACE inhibitor, with metabolic acidosis and rising creatinine from a recent normal baseline. Differentials include ATN from hypoperfusion or toxins, acute interstitial nephritis, and post-renal obstruction. Obtain urgent renal/bladder ultrasound and CK/myoglobin while continuing cardiac monitoring and hourly urine output; do not delay treatment for nonessential tests. Urgency is critical because of shock risk and malignant arrhythmia/sinusoidal ECG progression. Hold the ACE inhibitor and other nephrotoxins or potassium loads; avoid potassium-containing fluids; stabilize the membrane before waiting on dialysis access. Plan: IV calcium for myocardial protection, insulin–glucose shift, bicarbonate for severe acidosis, loop diuretics if volume-responsive, and urgent nephrology for emergent hemodialysis.
1.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Severe acute kidney injury (KDIGO Stage 3) complicated by critical hyperkalemia and potassium-induced myocardial toxicity. Top differential: Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN) due to hypoperfusion/toxins, Acute Interstitial Nephritis, Urinary tract obstruction (obstructive uropathy).

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Urgent renal and urinary tract ultrasound (to rule out post-renal/obstructive causes) and immediate serum myoglobin and CK levels (to rule out rhabdomyolysis). Continuous cardiac monitoring, vital signs tracking, and strict hourly urine output monitoring (via indwelling urinary catheter).

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical. Red flags: hemodynamic instability (hypotension), malignant ventricular arrhythmias or imminent cardiac arrest indicated by the ECG (QRS fusing with the T wave into a sinusoidal pattern), and persistent or worsening obtundation.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Immediately discontinue the ACE-inhibitor and any other potentially nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, potassium-sparing diuretics) or potassium supplements. Do not administer potassium-containing intravenous fluids (e.g., Lactated Ringer's). Do not delay myocardial stabilization therapy while waiting for dialysis placement.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Immediate myocardial stabilization with IV Calcium Gluconate 10% (10-20 mL over 5-10 min). Shift potassium intracellularly using an infusion of Hypertonic Dextrose + Regular Insulin (e.g., 25g glucose + 10 units insulin) and administer IV Sodium Bicarbonate due to the severe acidosis. Administer IV loop diuretics (Furosemide) if the patient is minimally responsive to fluid challenges. Urgent nephrology consultation for emergent hemodialysis.

2.title: Anaphylaxis with airway compromise
2.stem:
Patient: 27-year-old male.
History: Known IgE-mediated peanut allergy with prior anaphylaxis; carries epinephrine auto-injector. 20 minutes after eating takeout labeled peanut-free, developed diffuse pruritus, facial swelling, throat tightness, and wheezing. Used one 0.3 mg epinephrine auto-injector IM in the thigh with only partial improvement. On arrival, progressive dyspnea and lightheadedness. Takes propranolol 40 mg BID for migraine prophylaxis. No asthma diagnosis. No recent ACE inhibitor.
Physical Examination: Distressed, biphasic stridor, lip and tongue angioedema, widespread urticaria. BP 78/46 mmHg, HR 128 bpm, RR 32, SpO2 88% on room air improving to 92% on non-rebreather. Diffuse wheezes. Capillary refill 4 s. Alert but anxious.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Fingerstick glucose 102 mg/dL. Point-of-care lactate 3.8 mmol/L. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Portable chest X-ray pending. Serum tryptase drawn (result pending). ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO2 48 mmHg, PaO2 58 mmHg on NRB.
2.reference_prose: This is severe anaphylaxis after probable peanut exposure in a known allergic patient on propranolol, with airway compromise (stridor, angioedema), bronchospasm, hypoxia with rising CO2, and hypotensive shock only partly improved by one IM epinephrine dose. Differentials such as primary asthma, hereditary angioedema, foreign body, or sepsis are less fitting given urticaria plus hypotension and the allergic tempo. Do not delay epinephrine or airway management for labs; monitor continuously, support ABCs, and use ABG/lactate/ECG/tryptase as adjuncts once treatment is under way. Urgency is critical now. Give IM epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh immediately and repeat every few minutes if shock or airway threat persists; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only. Expect possible beta-blocker–refractory features and consider glucagon if shock continues after epinephrine and fluids; prepare early for a difficult airway and observe for biphasic reaction. Initial plan: IM epinephrine, oxygen, IV fluids, airway readiness, adjuncts after epinephrine, ICU observation, and discharge planning with auto-injectors plus allergy follow-up.
2.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Anaphylaxis (severe) with airway involvement (stridor, angioedema), bronchospasm, and distributive/hypotensive shock after probable peanut exposure; partial response to one IM epinephrine dose; beta-blocker therapy may contribute to refractory features. Top differential: acute severe asthma exacerbation (less likely as primary without asthma history and with urticaria/hypotension/angioedema), hereditary/acquired angioedema (no urticaria/hypotension typical), foreign-body airway obstruction, sepsis with laryngitis (tempo and urticaria argue against).

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Do not delay epinephrine/airway for labs. Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring; repeat vitals frequently; prepare for definitive airway. ABG/VBG as available; lactate; ECG already done; chest X-ray after stabilization if indicated; serum tryptase (ideally within ~1–3 h of onset, already drawn) for later confirmation; document allergen exposure for outpatient allergy follow-up.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical — treat as airway/breathing/circulation emergency now. Red flags: biphasic stridor, tongue/floor-of-mouth swelling, hypoxia with rising PaCO2, refractory hypotension, altered mentation, cardiac arrest risk, need for repeat epinephrine or escalation to airway.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Give IM epinephrine immediately into the anterolateral thigh; do not wait for IV access, antihistamines, or steroids. Antihistamines/steroids are adjuncts only — never first-line for airway/shock. Avoid relying on a single auto-injector if shock/airway persists — repeat IM epinephrine q3–5 min as needed. Patient is on propranolol: expect possible refractory hypotension/bronchospasm; if shock persists after epinephrine and fluids, consider IM/IV glucagon per protocol. Caution with IV epinephrine boluses in conscious patients (use monitored infusion if needed for refractory shock). Prepare early for difficult airway (angioedema) — most experienced airway operator, backup surgical airway. Observe for biphasic reaction after stabilization.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Immediate IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) anterolateral thigh; high-flow O2; large-bore IV access; rapid crystalloid bolus for hypotension; nebulized epinephrine and/or bronchodilator for lower-airway wheeze if needed; early airway decision if stridor/angioedema progresses; H1 antihistamine and corticosteroid as adjuncts after epinephrine; glucagon if beta-blocker–refractory shock; stop allergen exposure; ICU/monitored observation for biphasic anaphylaxis; prescribe ≥2 epinephrine auto-injectors and urgent allergy referral on discharge planning.

3.title: STEMI
3.stem:
Patient: 61-year-old male.
History: Long-standing type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia. Smokes 1 pack/day. Awoke at 05:30 with crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw, associated with diaphoresis and nausea. Pain ongoing for 90 minutes. No prior MI. Takes metformin and atorvastatin.
Physical Examination: Anxious, diaphoretic. BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 104 bpm regular, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air. Heart sounds S1/S2, no murmur. Lungs clear. No calf swelling.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Troponin I elevated at 2.4 ng/mL (URL 0.04). ECG: 3 mm ST-segment elevation in V2–V4 with reciprocal ST depression in II, III, aVF. Chest X-ray: no acute pulmonary edema.
3.reference_prose: This presentation is an anterior STEMI (LAD territory) with ongoing ischemic pain, clear ST elevation with reciprocal changes, and elevated troponin in a diabetic smoker. Unstable angina/NSTEMI, dissection, myopericarditis, or Takotsubo remain secondary considerations. Activate emergent angiography / primary PCI without waiting on nonessential testing; continue monitoring and complete cath-prep labs. This is a time-critical emergency with red flags for shock, arrhythmia, block, or refractory pain. Do not delay reperfusion; use antiplatelet/anticoagulation per ACS–PCI protocol and be cautious with nitrates if hypotensive. Plan: aspirin and protocol P2Y12/anticoagulation, oxygen only if hypoxemic, urgent primary PCI, CCU monitoring, then secondary prevention including smoking cessation.
3.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), anterior wall (LAD territory), Killip I; ongoing ischemic chest pain ~90 minutes. Top differential: unstable angina/NSTEMI with early ST changes, aortic dissection with coronary involvement (less likely without tearing/back pain or pulse deficit), myopericarditis, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Continuous cardiac monitoring; serial ECGs if symptoms change; repeat high-sensitivity troponin (does not delay reperfusion); basic metabolic panel, CBC, coagulation panel for cath; activate emergent coronary angiography / primary PCI pathway; CXR already done.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical / time-critical emergency — activate cath lab / STEMI pathway immediately (door-to-balloon target). Red flags: hypotension, acute heart failure/pulmonary edema, malignant arrhythmias (VT/VF), complete heart block, refractory pain, cardiogenic shock.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Do not delay reperfusion for nonessential testing or troponin confirmation. Caution with nitrates if hypotensive or RV infarct suspected (inferior pattern not primary here). Dual antiplatelet and anticoagulation per protocol before/during PCI. Watch for arrhythmias and cardiogenic shock. Hold metformin around contrast if AKI risk.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Aspirin (chewed) and P2Y12 / anticoagulation per local ACS–PCI protocol; oxygen only if hypoxemic; urgent primary PCI; ICU/CCU monitoring post-PCI; smoking cessation and secondary prevention counseling after stabilization.

4.title: DKA
4.stem:
Patient: 22-year-old female.
History: Known type 1 diabetes on insulin pump. 3 days of polyuria, polydipsia, and progressive nausea after a viral illness. Missed several bolus corrections. Today: vomiting, abdominal pain, and lethargy. No fever reported at home.
Physical Examination: Ill-appearing, dry mucous membranes. BP 96/60, HR 122, RR 28 with Kussmaul breathing, SpO2 98% RA, temp 37.1°C. Abdomen soft, diffusely tender without peritonitis. Fruity breath odor noted.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Glucose 482 mg/dL. VBG: pH 7.12, HCO3 8 mmol/L, anion gap 28. Serum ketones positive (beta-hydroxybutyrate elevated). K+ 5.6 mEq/L, Na 132, Cr 1.4 (baseline 0.7). WBC 14.2. Urinalysis: glucose 4+, ketones 3+.
4.reference_prose: A young adult with type 1 diabetes on a pump presents with moderate–severe DKA after illness and missed boluses: marked hyperglycemia, high anion-gap acidosis, ketonemia, volume depletion, and Kussmaul breathing. HHS or primary abdomen with secondary derangement are less likely. Trend glucose, gases, electrolytes (especially potassium), ketones, and ECG given hyperkalemia; culture if infection is suspected. Urgency is high/critical for prompt fluids and a DKA protocol in a unit that can lab frequently. Do not start insulin if potassium is below 3.3—replete first; watch cerebral edema risk and overly rapid osmolality shifts. Plan: isotonic resuscitation, protocolized insulin after potassium safety, add dextrose at the usual glucose threshold, replete electrolytes, treat the trigger, and review pump/education before discharge.
4.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Diabetic ketoacidosis (moderate–severe) precipitated by intercurrent illness / insulin omission; volume depletion; high anion-gap metabolic acidosis with ketonemia. Top differential: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (less likely with prominent ketosis/acidosis in young T1D), starvation ketosis with stress hyperglycemia, primary acute abdomen with secondary metabolic derangement.

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Fingerstick/serum glucose trending; serial VBG or ABG; electrolytes q2–4h especially potassium; beta-hydroxybutyrate; CBC; cultures if infection suspected; ECG given hyperkalemia; consider lipase if abdominal pain remains atypical after resuscitation.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: High/critical — start IV fluids and DKA protocol promptly; admit to ICU/step-down capable of frequent labs. Red flags: K <3.3 before insulin, deteriorating mental status (cerebral edema risk), refractory shock, severe hypokalemia during treatment.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Do not start insulin if potassium is <3.3 mEq/L—replete first. Monitor for cerebral edema (young adult). Avoid overly rapid sodium/osmolality shifts. Transition off insulin pump carefully. Maintain VTE risk awareness.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Isotonic fluid resuscitation then protocolized IV insulin infusion after potassium safety check; add dextrose when glucose falls to protocol threshold (~200–250 mg/dL); electrolyte repletion; identify/treat trigger; diabetes education and pump review before discharge.

5.title: Acute ischemic stroke
5.stem:
Patient: 72-year-old female.
History: Atrial fibrillation on apixaban (last dose this morning uncertain per family). Sudden-onset right-sided weakness and aphasia witnessed at 10:15. Arrives ED at 11:05 (50 minutes from onset). Hypertension, prior TIA.
Physical Examination: BP 178/98, HR 96 irregularly irregular, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, glucose 118 mg/dL. NIHSS 12: right hemiparesis, expressive aphasia, right facial droop. No seizure activity.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Non-contrast head CT: no hemorrhage. CTA head/neck pending. INR 1.1, creatinine 0.9, platelets normal.
5.reference_prose: This is a disabling acute ischemic stroke (aphasia and hemiparesis) last known well at 10:15, with atrial fibrillation as a possible embolic source and no hemorrhage on non-contrast CT. Todd’s paresis, ICH, hypoglycemia, and complex migraine are less likely. Complete vascular imaging (CTA ± perfusion) and thrombolysis/thrombectomy labs without delay; telemetry and swallow screen before oral intake. Hyperacute stroke-code urgency applies. Confirm last apixaban timing before IV thrombolysis, respect BP targets, keep NPO until swallow cleared. Plan: IV thrombolysis and/or endovascular therapy if eligible, stroke-unit care, timed anticoagulation restart after imaging, secondary prevention and early rehab.
5.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Acute ischemic stroke with disabling deficits (aphasia + hemiparesis), last known well 10:15; atrial fibrillation with possible cardioembolic source; no ICH on non-contrast CT. Top differential: seizure with Todd’s paresis (no witnessed seizure), intracranial hemorrhage (excluded on NCCT), hypoglycemia (glucose normal), complex migraine (less likely with AF and NIHSS 12).

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Immediate NCCT (done); CTA head/neck ± CT perfusion per protocol; labs for thrombolysis/thrombectomy eligibility; ECG/telemetry; swallow screen before oral intake.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical / hyperacute — stroke code; door-to-needle and endovascular decision within time windows; do not delay vascular imaging. Red flags: declining consciousness, airway compromise, hemorrhagic transformation signs, severe hypertension outside protocol targets.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Confirm anticoagulation / last apixaban dose before IV thrombolysis. Respect BP targets per protocol. Keep NPO until swallow cleared. Fall and aspiration precautions. Avoid hypotonic fluids.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: If eligible, IV thrombolysis and/or endovascular thrombectomy pathway; admit to stroke unit; time restart/optimization of anticoagulation after follow-up imaging; secondary prevention and early rehab.

6.title: Suicidal crisis with suspected TCA/SSRI overdose
6.stem:
Patient: 29-year-old female.
History: Major depression on amitriptyline 75 mg at bedtime and sertraline 100 mg daily. Partner found her unresponsive-appearing after she sent goodbye texts stating she intended to die and had taken "a lot of my nerve pills." Empty amitriptyline bottle nearby (≈60 × 25 mg missing); sertraline bottle also depleted. Time of ingestion uncertain (~1–3 hours). No known seizure. Prior suicide attempt 2 years ago. No alcohol co-ingestion reported.
Physical Examination: Awake but drowsy, tearful, cooperative when engaged. BP 98/62, HR 118 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, temp 37.0°C. Pupils midsize, sluggish. Dry mucous membranes. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. No focal neurologic deficit. Skin warm, no rigidity. 1:1 sitter at bedside; belongings searched.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Fingerstick glucose 94 mg/dL. ECG: sinus tachycardia 118; QRS 118 ms; QTc 490 ms; no definite Brugada-like pattern yet. VBG: pH 7.36, HCO3 22. Na 138, K 3.9, Cr 0.8. Acetaminophen and salicylate levels pending. Serum ethanol pending. Urine toxicology immunoassay pending. Pregnancy test negative.
6.reference_prose: This is an acute suicidal crisis with intentional overdose, most consistent with amitriptyline (TCA) ± sertraline co-ingestion, plus early cardiotoxicity signals (tachycardia, QRS widening, QTc prolongation) and high suicide intent. Isolated SSRI toxicity or “psych only” clearance without tox/cardiac workup would be unsafe. Need continuous monitoring, serial ECGs, electrolytes, acetaminophen/salicylate levels, and psychiatry after medical stabilization starts. Critical dual emergency — medical and behavioral. Maintain 1:1 observation; treat wide-complex TCA toxicity with sodium bicarbonate per protocol; avoid Ia/Ic agents and premature psych-ward transfer on an unstable ECG. Plan: ABCs, telemetry, bicarbonate for Na-channel blockade, seizure precautions, tox involvement, parallel suicide precautions, then urgent psychiatry and regimen revision once medically clear.
6.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Acute suicidal crisis with intentional overdose — likely amitriptyline (TCA) ± sertraline (SSRI) co-ingestion; early cardiotoxicity signals (sinus tachycardia, QRS widening toward ≥100–120 ms, QTc prolongation). Concurrent high acute suicide risk (intent, plan, goodbye texts, means). Top differential: isolated SSRI overdose/serotonin toxicity (less likely as sole driver without clonus/hyperreflexia/hyperthermia yet), mixed polypharmacy OD, primary arrhythmia/syncope mimic, medical clearance vs primary psychiatric presentation only (do not skip toxicologic/cardiac evaluation).

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Continuous cardiac monitoring and serial ECGs (QRS/QTc trend); repeat electrolytes (especially K/Mg); acetaminophen and salicylate levels (co-ingestions); ethanol; pregnancy already done; consider ABG if deteriorating; urine tox as adjunct only (does not rule out TCA). Do not delay decontamination/antidote decisions for immunoassay. Psychiatry consult after medical stabilization pathway initiated; collateral for remaining pills/time course.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical — simultaneous medical toxicology emergency and behavioral health emergency. Red flags: QRS ≥100–120 ms or widening, ventricular arrhythmias, seizures, declining GCS/airway risk, hypotension, rising QTc, hyperthermia/clonus suggesting serotonin toxicity, elopement or further self-harm attempts.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Maintain 1:1 observation and ligature-free environment; do not leave unattended for "psych only" disposition before medical clearance. For TCA toxicity: sodium bicarbonate for wide QRS / Na-channel blockade per ACLS/tox guidance; avoid class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics and avoid physostigmine; caution with antipsychotics that further prolong QTc until ECG stabilizes. Do not induce emesis. Activated charcoal only if early presentation, protected airway, and no contraindications. Avoid premature psychiatric ward transfer with unstable ECG. Screen for ongoing intent/plan; remove means.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: ABCs + continuous telemetry; IV access; treat wide-complex TCA cardiotoxicity with IV sodium bicarbonate boluses/infusion targeting narrowing QRS per protocol; correct electrolytes; benzodiazepines first-line for seizures; early airway if GCS falls. Poison control / toxicology involvement. Serial ECGs and observation for delayed TCA deterioration. Parallel suicide precautions (1:1, search, no sharps). After medical clearance criteria met, urgent psychiatry for involuntary hold assessment as indicated, safety planning, and antidepressant regimen revision (avoid unsupervised TCA restart).

7.title: First-episode psychosis vs delirium
7.stem:
Patient: 24-year-old male.
History: No prior psychiatric diagnosis. Over 5 days, family reports new auditory hallucinations (commenting voices), paranoid delusions that neighbors implanted a chip, severe insomnia, and agitation. Yesterday he was found wandering outside at night, disoriented to time. Today in ED he is intermittently inattentive and keeps falling asleep mid-sentence, then abruptly becomes fearful and tries to leave. No known drug use per family, but friends mention possible stimulant use at a party 1 week ago. Mild feverish feeling at home. No head trauma witnessed. Takes no medications.
Physical Examination: BP 148/90, HR 110, RR 20, SpO2 98% RA, temp 38.1°C. Appears ill/tired. Mucous membranes dry. Pupils midsize reactive. Neck supple (limited cooperation). Intermittent attention, fluctuating orientation; briefly follows commands then distractible. No frank focal motor deficit. Mild tremor. Skin: no diaphoresis/rigidity of NMS; no clear clonus. Agitated when approached; security present.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Glucose 108 mg/dL. Na 148, K 3.6, Cr 1.3, WBC 13.8, CK 420. AST/ALT mildly up. Urine tox immunoassay pending. Ethanol negative. ECG: sinus tach 110, QTc 445 ms. Non-contrast head CT pending. LP not done.
7.reference_prose: Treat this as acute encephalopathy with psychotic features — first-episode psychosis versus delirium/organic secondary psychosis until proven otherwise. Fever, fluctuating attention, possible stimulant exposure, and a subacute course favor a medical/tox/CNS workup even though primary schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis remains possible. Pursue CT, labs/tox, and low threshold for LP if encephalitic features persist; do not rely on psych-clearance labs alone. Urgency is high/critical for medical stabilization and safety. Do not heavily sedate and dump to psych while delirium or CNS infection remain open; protect patient and staff and be cautious with QTc-prolonging drugs. Parallel plan: medical workup and treat triggers; continuous observation and measured de-escalation; psychiatry for a first-episode pathway once life-threatening causes are addressed or co-managed.
7.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Acute encephalopathy with psychotic features — must treat as first-episode psychosis vs delirium/organic secondary psychosis until proven otherwise. Red flags for medical/delirium/tox cause: subacute-to-acute 5-day course, fluctuating attention/arousal, fever, tachycardia, possible stimulant exposure, mild metabolic derangement. Primary first-episode schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis remains on the differential but should not short-circuit medical workup. Top differential: stimulant/other intoxication or withdrawal, CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis), autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic encephalopathy, intracranial mass/bleed (less likely without focal signs), primary psychiatric first-episode psychosis.

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Fingerstick/serum glucose (done); BMP, CBC, LFTs, CK already started — add TSH, B12 as available; urine and appropriately timed serum toxicology; ECG (done). Non-contrast head CT now given altered/fluctuating mentation + new psychosis. Low threshold for LP after imaging if fever/encephalitic features persist (CNS infection/autoimmune workup). Consider EEG if nonconvulsive seizures suspected. Do not rely on "psych clearance" labs alone when delirium flags present.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: High/critical — medical workup and safety stabilization before assuming primary psychiatry. Red flags: progressive fever/meningismus, seizures, declining GCS, severe agitation with violence risk, hyperthermia/rigidity (NMS/serotonin), focal neuro deficits, inability to protect airway.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Do not sedate heavily and discharge to psych without addressing delirium/tox/CNS infection possibilities. Avoid premature high-dose antipsychotic monotherapy as the only intervention while fever/fluctuating attention remain unexplained. Use least restrictive safe environment; protect patient and staff from elopement/assault. Caution with QTc-prolonging agents and anticholinergic burden in possible toxidromes. If encephalitis suspected, do not delay LP/imaging for involuntary psych admission paperwork.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Parallel tracks: (1) medical — CT, labs/tox, consider LP ± acyclovir if encephalitis cannot be excluded, IV fluids, treat identifiable metabolic triggers; (2) safety — quiet room, continuous observation, verbal de-escalation, offer PO antipsychotic/benzo only as needed for dangerous agitation after ECG/tox context considered, IM options per protocol if imminent violence; (3) psychiatry consult for first-episode pathway once life-threatening medical causes addressed or co-managed. Document capacity/hold status; arrange medical admission (medicine/neuro) preferentially over pure psych ward if delirium/organic workup ongoing.

8.title: Septic shock (pneumonia)
8.stem:
Patient: 67-year-old male.
History: COPD on home oxygen 2 L/min; type 2 diabetes; chronic kidney disease stage 3 (baseline creatinine 1.6 mg/dL). Three days of productive cough, fever, and progressive dyspnea. Today family found him confused and diaphoretic. Last oral intake uncertain. No known drug allergies. Takes metformin, tiotropium, and albuterol PRN. No recent hospitalization.
Physical Examination: Ill-appearing, altered (oriented to person only). BP 78/42 mmHg, HR 124 bpm, RR 32, SpO2 86% on 2 L NC improving to 91% on non-rebreather, temp 38.9°C. Capillary refill 5 s; cool mottled extremities. Crackles and dullness over the right lower lobe. Abdomen soft. No rash.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Lactate 5.2 mmol/L. WBC 18.4 with left shift. Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL. Glucose 264 mg/dL. Platelets 98. VBG: pH 7.28, HCO3 16. Chest X-ray: dense right lower-lobe infiltrate. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Blood cultures not yet drawn. Antibiotics not yet given.
8.reference_prose: This is septic shock from community-acquired pneumonia with hypotension, elevated lactate, hypoxemia, and acute-on-chronic kidney injury—time-critical resuscitation, not a delayed ward workup. Differentials such as cardiogenic shock, PE, or COPD exacerbation alone fit less well given fever, focal infiltrate, and distributive shock physiology. Obtain blood (and preferably sputum) cultures before antibiotics when that does not delay the first dose; start broad empiric antibiotics immediately; give rapid crystalloid and escalate to vasopressors for persistent hypotension after fluids, aiming for source control of the pneumonia pathway and ICU-level care. Urgency is critical. Do not withhold the first antibiotic hour for imaging or culture logistics; watch for fluid overload in COPD/CKD and avoid delaying vasopressors once fluid-refractory; hold metformin in shock/AKI. Plan: cultures then immediate Abx, oxygen/airway support, fluids then norepinephrine as needed, serial lactate, early critical-care involvement.
8.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Septic shock secondary to community-acquired pneumonia (right lower-lobe infiltrate) with tissue hypoperfusion (lactate 5.2, hypotension, mottled extremities) and acute-on-chronic kidney injury. Top differential: cardiogenic shock / acute decompensated heart failure (less likely without pulmonary edema pattern or ischemic ECG primary), pulmonary embolism with shock, severe COPD exacerbation with hypercapnic failure alone (fever/infiltrate/lactate argue for infection-driven shock), hypovolemic shock from other occult loss.

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Draw blood cultures (ideally ≥2 sets) before antibiotics if that does not delay the first antibiotic dose; sputum culture if obtainable without delaying therapy; CBC/BMP already started — add LFTs/coags as available; serial lactate; continuous SpO2/telemetry; ABG/VBG for gas exchange/acid-base; ECG done; consider procalcitonin only as adjunct. Do not delay antibiotics for CT. Early ICU/critical-care notification.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical — treat as time-sensitive septic shock now (hour-1 bundle mindset). Red flags: refractory hypotension after fluids, rising lactate, worsening hypoxia/work of breathing, declining mentation, oliguria/worsening AKI, DIC/thrombocytopenia progression, need for mechanical ventilation or multiple vasopressors.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Do not delay the first antibiotic dose waiting for cultures, CT, or "admission labs." Obtain cultures before Abx only when immediately feasible. Avoid under-resuscitation, but also avoid indiscriminate massive fluids in COPD/CKD without reassessment — escalate to vasopressors for fluid-refractory shock. Hold metformin in shock/AKI. Caution with nephrotoxins. Secure airway early if fatigue or failure. Source-control mindset: treat pneumonia aggressively; reassess if atypical source emerges.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Immediate cultures then broad empiric IV antibiotics covering CAP/sepsis pathogens per local protocol within the first hour; high-flow O2 or escalate respiratory support; large-bore IV access; rapid crystalloid bolus with frequent reassessment, then norepinephrine for persistent hypotension; serial lactate and urine output; ICU admission; hold metformin; identify/treat source (pneumonia pathway) and escalate if no improvement.

9.title: Intermediate–high risk PE
9.stem:
Patient: 54-year-old female.
History: Recently completed a 10-hour flight 4 days ago. Active smoker. Combined oral contraceptive. Sudden-onset dyspnea and right pleuritic chest pain at home 2 hours ago; one brief syncopal prodrome (near-fainting) without witnessed seizure. No fever at onset. No prior VTE. No known malignancy. Arrives ED anxious and short of breath.
Physical Examination: Distressed, speaking in short sentences. BP 108/68 mmHg (initially 96/60 en route, improved with O2 and fluids), HR 118 bpm, RR 28, SpO2 89% on room air → 94% on 4 L NC, temp 37.0°C. Lungs: clear bilaterally, no wheezes, no crackles. Heart: loud P2, no murmur. Mild right calf swelling and tenderness. JVP mildly elevated.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: ABG on 4 L: pH 7.46, PaCO2 30 mmHg, PaO2 62 mmHg. Troponin I mildly elevated. BNP/NT-proBNP elevated. ECG: sinus tachycardia, incomplete RBBB, T-wave inversions V1–V3. Chest X-ray: clear (no infiltrate, no pulmonary edema). D-dimer pending. Bedside echo (ED): RV dilated with septal flattening; no pericardial effusion. CT pulmonary angiogram not yet done.
9.reference_prose: This presentation is intermediate–high-risk acute pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise: hypoxemia, clear lungs, RV strain on ECG/echo, biomarker elevation, and VTE risk (flight, OCP, smoking), with transient hypotension en route. Pneumonia and cardiogenic edema are less likely with a clear radiograph and no fever/crackles. Risk-stratify (hemodynamics, RV dysfunction, troponin/BNP), pursue definitive imaging (CTPA if stable enough; consider V/Q or empiric therapy only if imaging truly unavailable and suspicion is high), support oxygenation, and start anticoagulation promptly once PE is confirmed or when pretest probability is high and bleeding risk is acceptable while arranging imaging. Consider thrombolysis or advanced therapy if frank shock or deterioration develops; otherwise anticoagulation plus monitoring is the usual intermediate–high pathway. Urgency is high/critical. Do not treat as simple pneumonia or withhold anticoagulation for nonessential delays when PE is the working diagnosis and bleed risk is low; avoid thrombolysis in a still-normotensive patient without clear high-risk features or specialist pathway. Plan: O2, urgent CTPA, parenteral anticoagulation, ICU/step-down monitoring, escalate if shock returns.
9.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Acute pulmonary embolism, intermediate–high risk (hypoxemia, RV dysfunction on bedside echo/ECG, elevated troponin/BNP, transient prehospital hypotension, strong VTE risks). Top differential: community-acquired pneumonia / pleuritis (less likely with clear CXR and no fever), acute coronary syndrome / RV infarct, acute heart failure / flash pulmonary edema (clear lungs/CXR argue against), pneumothorax, primary arrhythmia with syncope.

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Urgent CT pulmonary angiogram if hemodynamically acceptable (definitive pathway); continuous telemetry and SpO2; formal echo if bedside limited; CBC, BMP, coagulation panel before anticoagulation; troponin/BNP already elevated — trend; ECG serial if symptoms change. D-dimer does not delay CTPA in high pretest probability. If CT contraindicated/unavailable and suspicion remains very high, discuss empiric anticoagulation and alternative imaging (V/Q) per protocol.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: High/critical — time-sensitive imaging and anticoagulation; ICU/step-down capable monitoring. Red flags: recurrent hypotension/shock, worsening hypoxia or RV failure, syncope/arrest, hemoptysis with anticoagulation decisions, need for thrombolysis or embolectomy pathway.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Do not mislabel as pneumonia/edema and delay PE workup when CXR is clear and RV strain is present. Screen bleeding risk before anticoagulation/thrombolysis. Avoid routine systemic thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE that remains normotensive without deterioration — reserve for high-risk/shock or selected intermediate–high cases per protocol/specialist. Confirm PE (or accept very high probability + low bleed risk) before lytics. Caution with fluids if RV is overloaded; support BP carefully. Stop OCP counseling after stabilization.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: Oxygen to correct hypoxemia; urgent CTPA; start parenteral anticoagulation (e.g., heparin pathway) once PE confirmed or when indicated by high probability + acceptable bleed risk while imaging arranged; continuous monitoring for hemodynamic collapse; involve critical care / PE response if RV strain + instability; escalate to thrombolysis or advanced reperfusion only if shock/arrest or protocolized intermediate–high deterioration; admit monitored bed and address provoked-VTE counseling (OCP, travel).

10.title: Unstable upper GI bleed
10.stem:
Patient: 71-year-old male.
History: Known peptic ulcer disease years ago; heavy daily alcohol use; atrial fibrillation on apixaban (last dose last night). Melena for 24 hours, then large-volume hematemesis this morning with near-syncope. Takes occasional ibuprofen for knee pain. No prior variceal bleed documented. Arrives pale and sweaty.
Physical Examination: Awake but anxious. BP 86/50 mmHg, HR 118 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temp 36.6°C. Cool clammy skin; delayed capillary refill. Abdomen soft, epigastric tenderness, no peritonitis. No stigmata of chronic liver disease obvious to exam (no large ascites). Melena on rectal exam. Dual large-bore IVs placed.
Laboratory and Diagnostic Results: Hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL (baseline ~13 last month). Platelets 142. INR 1.3. BUN 48, creatinine 1.4. Lactate 3.1 mmol/L. Type and screen pending. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray pending. Nasogastric aspiration not yet performed.
10.reference_prose: This is an unstable upper GI bleed with hemorrhagic shock features (hematemesis, melena, hypotension, tachycardia, acute anemia) in a patient on apixaban with ulcer and NSAID risks—resuscitate first, then definitive endoscopy. Variceal bleed remains on the differential given alcohol use even without florid chronic-liver stigmata. Priority tests: type and crossmatch, serial hemoglobin, coagulation/platelet context, lactate, ECG; risk scores (e.g., Glasgow-Blatchford / clinical Rockall) support disposition urgency but do not replace ABC care. Urgency is critical. Reverse anticoagulation when bleeding is life-threatening per protocol; start IV PPI; avoid delaying endoscopy for unstable patients who need airway protection and transfusion; do not give unnecessary massive crystalloid without blood products when hemorrhage is ongoing. Plan: aggressive resuscitation/transfusion, PPI, anticoag reversal as indicated, urgent GI endoscopy, ICU monitoring, hold NSAID/apixaban until secure hemostasis.
10.gold_raw:
Q1 [diagnosis]: What is the most likely primary diagnosis? Rank the top differential.
A1: Unstable acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding with hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock — likely peptic ulcer (prior PUD, NSAID) with apixaban coagulopathy contribution; alcohol use keeps variceal bleeding on the differential. Top differential: esophageal variceal hemorrhage, Mallory-Weiss tear, aortoenteric fistula (less likely without aortic history), lower GI bleed with vigorous hematochezia mimicking UGI (history favors upper), myocardial ischemia secondary to anemia/shock.

Q2 [tests]: Which tests should be ordered next?
A2: Type and crossmatch (activate massive-transfusion preparedness as needed); serial CBC/hemoglobin; BMP already started; coagulation panel/INR; lactate trend; ECG (done) — troponin if ischemic symptoms; liver tests if varices/liver disease suspected. Formal risk stratification (Glasgow-Blatchford ± clinical Rockall) for urgency/disposition. Do not delay resuscitation for endoscopy suite logistics. Early GI and ICU notification.

Q3 [urgency]: Urgency level (critical / high / moderate / low) and red flags.
A3: Critical — unstable GI hemorrhage; resuscitate and arrange urgent endoscopy. Red flags: refractory hypotension, ongoing hematemesis with airway threat, falling hemoglobin, rising lactate, altered mentation, need for massive transfusion, suspected varices with failure to control bleeding.

Q4 [safety]: Critical contraindications or safety traps.
A4: Protect airway early if ongoing hematemesis/obtundation — do not send an unprotected airway to endoscopy. Reverse apixaban / manage anticoagulation for life-threatening bleed per protocol (andexanet/PCC pathways as locally available) rather than ignoring DOAC effect. Avoid indiscriminate large crystalloid-only resuscitation when blood products are indicated. Caution with over-transfusion targets in stable variceal physiology if that pathway dominates later; here instability justifies blood. Hold NSAIDs and anticoagulants. Do not delay endoscopy in the unstable patient for nonessential imaging.

Q5 [plan]: Outline the initial management plan.
A5: ABCs; two large-bore IVs (done) ± central access if needed; crystalloid bridge then RBC transfusion toward hemodynamic stability (massive-transfusion protocol if exsanguinating); IV PPI bolus then infusion; reverse anticoagulation for life-threatening hemorrhage per protocol; NPO; urgent gastroenterology for emergent upper endoscopy (airway-protected); ICU monitoring; treat as possible variceal bleed with early vasoactive therapy/antibiotics if cirrhosis/varices become likely; hold apixaban/NSAIDs and plan timed restart only after hemostasis and thrombosis risk review.
